I can only speak for myself, in the absence of any other comments. British politics has never been more stale, and there's never been so little distance between the policies of the main three parties. It seems to me that the public have never felt so disenfranchised by and indifferent to politicians. I share this sentiment, particularly the perception that the main leaders all come from the same privileged background ultimately to further the same causes of influential lobbyists and their own self-interest.

I mean, let's look at them:

  • Cameron. A waxen, plasticky caricature of a leader, an Eton-bred template Tory with just the absolute bare minimum of charisma to get by, presiding over a set of policies, which as usual for the New Right, are a systematic and repeated punch in the face to the poor and the marginalised within society. The privatisation from within of the NHS is proceeding on track, and the public have been made to bail out the banks whilst being told to make-do and mend till this all blows over. Similarly, those dole scroungers have been ruthlessly culled, even the ones who'd like to be in work rather than being vilified in some latter-day Medieval witch hunt.

  • 'Ed' Milliband. Whilst Cameron commands the bare minimum of charisma, there's no danger of 'Ed' over-powering us with such insubstantial concepts as 'personality'. Although he went to a comprehensive school, as did myself some considerable time ago, he is very much a part of the political establishment. He has a Marxist upbringing and yet oversees the most moderate and centrist Labour manifesto in history. To vote for 'Ed' is to vote for Tory policies with softer edges. I think the Labour party had had a collective stroke when they chose him as leader over his far less spoddy and more experienced brother. The question I come back to is 'could we send Ed Milliband over to the USA to discuss important state matters and expect him to command any respect or authority in negotiations?' He gave a cringe-worthy speech recently about how he was 'ready' to be Prime Minister. I contend he's not done yet and he needs to go back in the oven for at least another five years.

  • Nick Clegg. Whilst not a full-blown Eton-ian, Clegg did nonetheless attend Cambridge University, which needs no explanation as to its status as a University. Again, maybe even more than Milliband or Cameron, it's hard to discern just who he is as a person, much less identify a single Lib Dem policy. A camera gets pointed at him, the mouth moves and the eyes stare in the right direction but there just doesn't seem to be anybody there. Whatever the Lib Dems stood for before the coalition has been trashed by the sheer absurdity of being in coalition with the Tories. I was watching a Lib Dem party-political the other day. All three main parties have done their bit in terms of negative campaigning, but I was disappointed still to see the Lib Dems doing it too, when it was absolutely the worst strategy they could've adopted. If the Tories want to attack the competition, they attack Labour. Labour, vice-versa. The Lib Dems spent two thirds of their slot trashing the other two before they even got to their own policies, a dumb own-goal when they should be making very clear what they themselves believe in.

  • Farage. Pipe and slippers politics nurturing an atmosphere of convivial bloke-in-pub agreement on matters of Johnny Foreigner. From the bargain-basement branding, to Farage's own simpering, tobacco-stained smile, everything is designed to deter accusations of being too slick, and foster a sense of being in touch with 'the average man', whoever that is. It's amusing on a shallow level but deeply disturbing when you consider his platform involves attempting to pretend globalisation hasn't happened by way of sticking the middle finger up at those 'eurocrats' in Brussels. And massively shrinking our overseas export potential in the process. And losing all influence over Europe.
